subsection.title: Page 1: What is an Ordinary Differential Equation?
subsection.p: In MATH 340, we study how phenomena change over time by modeling them using functions. We begin by looking at a differentiable function x with respect to a single independent variable t (representing time).

An equation that relates an unknown function x to its derivatives—such as \frac{dx}{dt}, \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}, and so on—is called an ordinary differential equation (ODE). The primary goal of an ODE is to describe a relationship where the rate of change of a quantity depends on the current state of that quantity.

To classify these equations, we define the order of an ODE as the highest derivative present in the equation. For example, a first-order ODE contains at most \frac{dx}{dt}, while a second-order ODE involves \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}.

subsection.title: Page 2: Analyzing ODE Structure and Notation
subsection.p: Consider a classic example of a simple first-order ordinary differential equation: \frac{dx}{dt} = x This equation states that the rate of growth of the function x(t) is directly equal to the value of the function itself at any moment in time.

When studying these structures, we will approach them using three distinct frameworks:
Numerical methods to approximate data tracks when explicit formulas are impossible to find.
Analytic methods to compute exact mathematical expressions for the unknown functions.
Qualitative methods to describe the long-term behavior and stability profiles of solutions visually.

subsection.title: Page 3: Recognizing and Verifying Solutions
subsection.p: A solution to a differential equation is an explicit function x(t) that, when substituted into the ODE, satisfies the algebraic identity for all values of t in an open interval.

statement.p: Verify that the solution function x(t) = e^t is a valid solution to the first-order ordinary differential equation \frac{dx}{dt} = x.

solution.p: To check if the function satisfies the relation, we evaluate both sides of the ODE independently:
First, compute the left-hand side (LHS) by differentiating our candidate function: \text{LHS} = \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(e^t\right) = e^t
Next, evaluate the right-hand side (RHS) by substituting the function directly: \text{RHS} = x = e^t
Since \text{LHS} = \text{RHS} = e^t, the function x(t) = e^t is verified as a valid explicit solution to the differential equation.
